title: US payrolls miss badly, trimming odds of an October Fed hike
content:
US nonfarm payrolls rose by only **29,000** in September against a consensus of roughly 84,000, while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2%. August was revised down to a gain of 133,000, and July and August were cut by a combined 60,000 jobs.

UST yields retreated, with the 10-year falling about 6bp to **5.18%** after touching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week, and the 2-year easing to around 4.73%. CME FedWatch showed the probability of an unchanged Fed decision in October rising to roughly 84%. Stock futures firmed, with Nasdaq benchmarks near record highs. The data complicates the Fed's inflation-fighting narrative, though elevated yields and oil prices limit the relief.

title: Global bond sell-off holds near multi-decade highs despite softer data
content:
Long-dated government bond yields hit fresh cycle highs this week, even after a benign inflation report and soft US jobs data. The 30-year UST yield reached roughly **5.6%**, its highest since 2002, according to reports, while 30-year gilt yields have traded near 5.9% and Japan's 10-year JGB yield has crossed 3% for the first time since 1996.

Drivers cited include fiscal concerns in the UK and France, BoJ policy repricing and inflation fears linked to higher energy prices. Bund yields are also at their highest since 2011. Equities have been resilient, led by megacap technology, but rate-sensitive sectors and small caps remain pressured, and sustained higher term premia could tighten financial conditions globally.

title: Brent holds near $100/bbl as US-Iran talks and G7 reserve plans pull in opposite directions
content:
Brent crude rose about 0.4% to roughly **$102.70/bbl** on 2 October, having eased from last week's rally towards $104 as Pakistan-mediated US-Iran talks revived hopes of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Doubts persist over whether the negotiations are viable.

Separately, the G7 agreed to consider releasing up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves to ease fuel costs. Elevated energy prices remain a key driver of inflation expectations and the global bond sell-off, so any breakdown in talks or fresh attacks on regional infrastructure could quickly push crude higher, while a credible deal would likely ease pressure on yields and central banks.
